newsitem.title: MEXICO: Family says Mexico's most wanted drug lord dead.
newsitem.headline: Family says Mexico's most wanted drug lord dead.

text.p: Mexico's most wanted drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes has died of a heart attack, his mother said on Saturday. Officials could not confirm the report.

Aurora Fuentes de Carrillo told reporters gathered at her luxury ranch in the village of Guamuchilito in northwestern Sinaloa state that rumours of her son's death, which began circulating on Friday night, were true.
Sinaloa police told Reuters they were investigating reports Carrillo's body was at the San Martin funeral parlour in the state capital of Culiacan.

Large red floral wreaths, some from rival drug traffickers, arrived at the home of the drug capo's mother, who told reporters her fugitive son had died during surgery at a hospital in Mexico City, radio network Radio Red said.
Mexico's Attorney General's Office said it could not confirm Carrillo's death until it had examined a corpse.
"Until now, although people close to Mr. Carrillo Fuentes have supposedly confirmed the news, the Attorney General's office is unable to confirm the reports," the statement said.
"This confirmation must wait until we have had access to the corpse and there has been a medical examination," it said.

Juan Blanco, the San Martin funeral parlour's director, told Mexico City's Radio Red that forensic experts were checking a body which arrived from Mexico City earlier in the day under the name Antonio Flores Montes.

"The man is in his 40's, robust-looking and well-dressed," Blanco said, adding he had received telephone instructions on Friday from an unidentified man telling him to pick up the body at the Culiacan airport on Saturday.
A steady stream of expensively-dressed men in luxury vehicles brought the floral wreaths to the home of Carrillo's mother, radio reports added.

They said some of the wreaths were signed by other notorious Mexican drug capos, including Hector "The Blonde" Palma, serving a six-year sentence on weapons charges in a Mexican jail, and Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman, the jailed head of the feared Sinaloa cartel.
Carrillo, believed to be 42, heads the so-called Juarez cartel, based in the northern border city of Ciudad Juarez, next to El Paso, Texas.

The cocaine baron's power grew during the late 1980s to almost legendary levels. He earned the nickname "Lord of the Skies" for his ability to fly cocaine-laden commercial jets undetected from South America to Mexico.

Thomas Constantine, the head of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), described Carrillo in June 1996 as "the most powerful figure in the Mexican drug trade". Carrillo was the subject of at least 26 separate DEA investigations.

The capo has already had several narrow escapes. He was arrested in 1989 but later released. In November 1993 he made a dramatic escape when rival mobsters tried to gun him down as he dined with his family in Mexico City's Bali-Hai restaurant.

Since he went underground, few pictures of Carrillo exist. The most recent were images from a video shot at his sister's wedding in January, showing the portly trafficker attending the ceremony dressed in a jacket and tie and hugging his wife.
Efforts to catch the elusive capo proved fruitless for some eight years, exposing the government to criticism from U.S. lawmakers that it was not doing enough to fight drugs.
The last known operation against him was at his sister's wedding, when soldiers and police stormed the reception in the Guamuchilito ranch but failed to find their prey.
An army major was later arrested for having allegedly tipped off the drug lord and allowing him to escape.

Carrillo's huge wealth allowed him to bribe scores of Mexican officials. Mexico's former anti-drugs chief, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, was jailed in February on charges he had taken bribes from Carrillo.
